findings.text: Participants reported actual overall timelines of roughly 2-6 months in practice: one described ~2 weeks for drawings, up to 3 months for soil testing, and 1 month at AMC (~5 months total); for big structures "at least 6 months."
Soil testing was named the single biggest pain point: mandatory, conducted offline outside OBPS, taking 3-4 months in high seismic/hazard-map zones and costing roughly ₹20,000-50,000.
AMC's review board sits only twice a month; any objection means corrections, resubmission and waiting for the next month's sitting.
OBPS is a one-way portal: applicants cannot type remarks or responses to officials, only upload additional documents.
Scrutiny was described as superficial: officials raise corrections for items already shown in the drawing, with generic, non-specific deficiency remarks, forcing repeated correction cycles.
Buildings above 16m require an additional structural/technical review board, extending timelines for big structures to 6+ months.
Building permission is currently valid for 3 years; renewing beyond that attracts a late fee of about ₹10/day and repeats the full process; participants felt the validity period should be increased.
AMC fees vary with built-up area (roughly ₹1,200 up to 100 sq m to ₹2,000 above 1,000 sq m; other cases ₹5,000-10,000) and are not seen as a major burden.
Make OBPS a two-way system so applicants can type observations/responses to officials, which participants believe would shorten the timeline.
Merge the offline soil-testing process into the single online approval system, with data fetched automatically by the government.
Make deficiency remarks specific rather than generalised, and scrutinise drawings properly rather than superficially.
Allow licensed technical professionals to self-certify/approve (risk-based inspection), with accountability fixed.
Increase the validity period of building permission beyond the current 3 years.
Fire department clearance adds about 2 additional weeks; full permission is granted only once the fire extinguisher has been installed.
Most participants are individual civil/structural-engineer practitioners who prepare drawings and file applications themselves without a separate consultant.
Direct government fees are not a major concern for participants; soil-testing cost and delay are the dominant cost driver.
Login to OBPS is restricted to the licensed technical person (consultants cannot log in on the applicant's behalf), and fees are paid online with no bank/office visit needed for payment.

gaps.text: ED cites a 30-day notified timeline with a deemed-approval provision (Reg. 7) activating after 30 days; FGD participants report actual timelines of 2-6 months (commonly ~5 months) with no participant mentioning ever invoking or being aware of the deemed-approval provision, suggesting it is not used despite frequent, large timeline overruns.

ED's documented steps/documents for BPA make no mention of a mandatory soil test; FGD participants describe soil testing as a mandatory, offline, 3-4 month, ₹20,000-50,000 step that is the single biggest driver of delay and cost — a significant process step absent from the ED record.

ED's validity record describes an amendment extending building-plan validity to 5 years (text partly garbled); FGD participants instead describe the current validity as 3 years, with a ₹10/day late fee for renewal beyond that — no participant referenced a 5-year validity.

FGD's cited fee range (~₹1,200 up to 100 sq m to ₹2,000 above 1,000 sq m; other cases ₹5,000-10,000) does not closely match ED's fee schedule (₹100-2,000 ground floor plus ₹200-4,000 per additional storey); both sources flag their own figures as approximate/garbled, so the discrepancy could not be resolved.

The ED record does not mention a Fire Department clearance as part of the Building Plan Approval chain, but FGD participants describe fire clearance (~2 additional weeks, full permission only after fire-extinguisher installation) as a necessary step before final approval.

findings.text: The respondent described the application as submitted fully online with the portal easy to use ("everything was smooth enough"), including online fee payment with no office visit needed.

Non-fee compliance costs (biomedical-waste segregation set-up, equipment purchases, monthly staff training) were reported at "more than ₹2,00,000, maybe more" — well beyond the nominal government fee.
Treatment-plant size/capacity requirements were not made clear upfront; they surfaced only at inspection, after the applicant had already built to its own estimate, prompting possible rework.
The respondent felt one-size-fits-all requirements are unnecessary for small facilities with limited environmental impact and should be scaled by facility size.
No real-time online application tracking exists; status is followed up only by telephone, named as the single biggest pain point.
Introduce online real-time tracking of application status instead of telephone follow-up.
Publish clear capacity/size norms for treatment plants upfront so facilities build to the right specification the first time.
Apply proportionate, size-based compliance requirements — relaxed for small facilities, stricter for large ones.
The application was prepared in-house; engineers/architects were consulted informally, mostly free of cost or for a token amount (about ₹1,000).
Government fees were considered nominal; no late fees or penalties were reported.
Overall approval time was about one month; the process was new to the respondent but completed without major delay.
The respondent disagreed with the inspector's view that the treatment plant was too small and felt the applicant must verify and potentially push back on inspection findings.

A participant's view that strict enforcement/inspections make compliance easier echoes the ED's description of advance multi-channel inspection communication, corroborating a largely cooperative, non-adversarial inspection regime from the business side.

findings.text: Dependence on engineers/consultants was named the biggest pain point by all participants — owners must wait for engineering consultancy to schedule survey, drawings and structure work, and good engineers are often busy in other districts.
Fire NOC cannot move without AMC building permission first; one participant had waited 7 months for AMC permission and met the AMC Commissioner multiple times.
Buildings above 5 storeys require a master's-degree structural engineer, and such engineers are in short supply, adding delay.
AMC's municipal committee sits only once a month, so a file missing one sitting must wait a full month.

Renewal was described as harder than the first application — officials ask why work was not completed on time, and extra signatures are needed from the local council (Taluk Chairman) and the engineer.
Participants mentioned some mutual "understanding" with inspection field staff is sometimes needed, and referenced costs that cannot be recorded in the books.
Application and documents are submitted online; one participant said filing itself can take about one day online.
Land revenue/land records are requested again by the inspection team after online submission; participants felt these could instead be fetched automatically by government.
Building drawings must be separately prepared and approved at AMC and then again presented for Fire NOC — a duplicated drawing-approval step across departments.

Charges depend on building area and type (separate rates for hospitals, offices, etc.) and are not clearly communicated to applicants in advance; large sites (23 or 45 buildings) each need a separate layout.
NOC validity ranges from about 6 months to 3 years depending on the case; no annual fee, only at renewal.
Participants agreed fire-fighting equipment is a must for safety and worth the cost, with rates fixed by government.
Reduce government fees/revenue charges where possible.
Fetch land/revenue records and other documents automatically rather than through repeated manual handling.
Make renewal lighter than the first application, with fewer signatures and questions.
Increase the availability of qualified structural engineers, or review the master's-degree requirement for buildings above 5 storeys.
Hold municipal committee sittings more often so files do not wait a month.
No dedicated grievance cell or helpline desk was identified by participants.

deemedApproval.text: No deemed-approval provision was reported, and participants said they are unsure of the prescribed renewal period. Separately, participants described a de facto enforcement gap: a business can continue operating with an expired licence without penalty or government follow-up, though this is an enforcement lapse rather than a stated deeming provision.

gaps.text: No clear rupee figure for the renewal fee is established — a '₹10,000' figure and a '₹50' per day/week charge were both mentioned but the transcript does not clarify what either refers to.
Payment mode at renewal (cash vs UPI) was asked about but the participant's answer is unclear in the transcript.
No notified/prescribed renewal timeline is known even to the participants themselves ('we do not know the prescribed period'), so no official SLA could be captured from this source.
Only the original licence is required for renewal, with no additional documentation burden reported.
Participants' strongest ask — moving renewal and payment online with SMS/WhatsApp expiry reminders — remains unimplemented per this transcript.

findings.text: Pipeline-laying/connection was identified as the stage consuming most of the time; the overall process was said to take "about a month."
Application submission through to approval is done fully offline; a participant felt an online mode could save time and transport cost.
Participants referred to multiple follow-up visits to the office, though an exact visit count for a new connection was not given.
An occasional office visit is needed when a bill is too high due to meter-reading errors — a billing issue rather than a new-connection issue.
No validity or expiry period applies to a water connection once supplied — the connection and pipeline remain in place indefinitely.
Fees are described as affordable and the same for commercial and residential connections; participants did not seek a reduction.
No equipment/infrastructure purchase was demanded of applicants; technical requirements were communicated clearly.
Documentation required is minimal — typically just a house pass/property document — with no additional documents or clarification demanded after submission.
The process is simple enough to be done without an intermediary, consultant or advisor.
Bill payment can be made both online (UPI) and offline (cash at the office).
A grievance mechanism exists — complaints (e.g., on high bills) are taken to the office and addressed from time to time.
No participant could recall an inspection being carried out for their connection.
Introduce an online option for application, status tracking and payment to save time and transport cost.
Several participants had old connections or did not apply personally, so could not comment on recent timelines, limiting the precision of this record.
